message.reasoning:
We need to write a JUnit 4 test file TokeniserStateTest.java that comprehensively tests all methods in TokeniserState. Since TokeniserState is an enum with many states and static methods. We need to mock or create a Tokeniser and CharacterReader to test behavior. However, the actual Tokeniser class is complex; we can create a minimal stub that records calls like emit, transition, error, etc. Use a fake Tokeniser that implements needed methods used by TokeniserState.read. We need to test read for each state, ensuring correct transitions and emitted tokens.

Simplify: create a MockTokeniser class with fields: List<Object> emitted = new ArrayList<>(); List<TokeniserState> transitions = new ArrayList<>(); StringBuilder dataBuffer = new StringBuilder(); TagPending stub etc. But many methods like createTagPending, tagPending.appendTagName, etc. We can create a simple inner class TagPending with fields to capture name, attributes, selfClosing, etc.

Simplify further: For many states we can test only a subset that doesn't require full tag handling. But requirement: comprehensively test all methods in TokeniserState. That includes read for each enum constant, and static helper methods: handleDataEndTag, readData, readCharRef, readEndTag, handleDataDoubleEscapeTag. So we need tests for each.

We can design a MockTokeniser that implements all methods used: advanceTransition, transition, emit (overloaded for String, char, int[], Token.EOF, Token.Comment, etc.), error, eofError, createTagPending, tagPending, dataBuffer, etc. Provide minimal behavior.

Simplify: For states that involve tagPending, we can have a simple TagPending class with methods used: appendTagName(String), appendTagName(char), newAttribute, appendAttributeName(String), appendAttributeName(char), appendAttributeValue(String), appendAttributeValue(int[]), setEmptyAttributeValue, etc., and fields to capture.

Also methods: createCommentPending, commentPending, etc.

But many states use many methods; implementing all may be large but doable.

Alternative: Use Mockito to mock Tokeniser and CharacterReader. But we need to verify interactions. However, many methods are called with arguments; we can verify using Mockito verify. That may be easier: create mock Tokeniser and mock CharacterReader, set up behavior for methods like current(), matchesLetter(), etc., and verify that appropriate methods are called.

But static methods like readData call r.consumeToAny etc., which we need to stub.

Using Mockito, we can create a mock CharacterReader with stubbed methods returning predetermined values. For each state, we set up the mock to simulate a scenario and then call TokeniserState.X.read(mockTokeniser, mockReader). Then verify that tokeniser methods were called as expected.

We need to test each branch.

Given the complexity, we can write tests for a representative subset of branches for each state, ensuring coverage.

We'll use Mockito (need dependency). In JUnit 4, we can use @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class) or MockitoAnnotations.initMocks(this). We'll import static org.mockito.Mockito.*.

We'll create a mock Tokeniser and mock CharacterReader.

We'll also need to stub static fields like TokeniserState.nullChar etc. But they are constants.

We'll need to stub Tokeniser.replacementChar? It's static final char in Tokeniser class; we don't need to reference.

We'll need to stub Tokeniser methods: advanceTransition(TokeniserState), transition(TokeniserState), emit(Object), error(TokeniserState), eofError(TokeniserState), createTagPending(boolean), createTagPending(boolean) returns Tag (we can mock Tag). But we can just stub createTagPending to return a mock Tag object.

Simplify: For methods that return something, we can have mock returns.

We'll need to stub tokeniser.tagPending to be a mock Tag with methods used.

But tokeniser.tagPending is a field accessed directly; we can set tokeniser.tagPending = mockTag.

Thus we need a concrete class for Tokeniser (or a mock with fields). Since Tokeniser is a class (not interface), we can create a subclass FakeTokeniser extends Tokeniser? But Tokeniser likely has many dependencies; easier to create a simple stub class that implements the same methods but not extend Tokeniser. However, TokeniserState.read expects a Tokeniser type, not an interface. So we need a class that extends Tokeniser or we can use a mock of Tokeniser (Mockito can mock concrete classes). Yes, we can mock Tokeniser class using Mockito.mock(Tokeniser.class). That will create a mock with all methods stubbed.

But tokeniser.tagPending is a field, not a method; accessing tokeniser.tagPending directly will not work on a mock because fields are not mocked. However, the code accesses tokeniser.tagPending directly (e.g., t.tagPending.appendTagName). Since tokeniser is a mock, its fields are null, leading to NullPointerException. So we need a real subclass that provides fields.

Thus we need to create a minimal FakeTokeniser class that mimics Tokeniser's fields and methods used. We'll define fields: TokeniserState currentState; List<Object> emitted = new ArrayList<>(); StringBuilder dataBuffer = new StringBuilder(); Tag tagPending; Comment commentPending; Doctype doctypePending; etc. Provide methods: advanceTransition(state) { transition(state); }, transition(state) { currentState = state; }, emit(Object o) { emitted.add(o); }, error(state) { }, eofError(state) { }, createTagPending(boolean start) { tagPending = new Tag(start); return tagPending; }, createCommentPending() { commentPending = new Token.Comment(); return commentPending; }, createDoctypePending() { doctypePending = new Token.Doctype(); return doctypePending; }, etc. Provide minimal Tag class with fields and methods used: StringBuilder name = new StringBuilder(); boolean selfClosing; List<Attribute> attributes = new ArrayList<>(); methods: appendTagName(String), appendTagName(char), newAttribute(), appendAttributeName(String), appendAttributeName(char), appendAttributeValue(String), appendAttributeValue(int[]), setEmptyAttributeValue(), etc.

Also need methods: consumeCharacterReference(char, boolean) used in readCharRef and attribute value states. For simplicity, we can have FakeTokeniser.consumeCharacterReference returning null.

Also methods: appropriateEndTagName(), isAppropriateEndTagToken(), etc., used in some states. Provide simple implementations returning null/false.

Also methods: emitTagPending() which adds tagPending to emitted list.

Also methods: emitCommentPending().

Also methods: emitDoctypePending().

Also methods: emit(String data) for data.

Also methods: emit(new Token.EOF()).

Also methods: emit(int[] chars) for char refs.

Also methods: emit(char) maybe.

Simplify: In emit(Object) we just add to list; for char we can wrap as Character.

Now we can test.

We'll need Token, Token.Comment, Token.Doctype, Token.EOF classes from jsoup. They exist. We'll import org.jsoup.parser.Token.

Now write test methods.

Example: testDataStateWithAmpersand: set up CharacterReader mock to return '&' for current, and ensure tokeniser.advanceTransition called with CharacterReferenceInData.

We'll need a mock CharacterReader with methods: current(), consume(), consumeData(), consumeToAny(...), etc. For this test, we only need current() and maybe others not called. So we can mock.

We'll use when(reader.current()).thenReturn('&'); then call TokeniserState.Data.read(fakeTokeniser, reader); verify fakeTokeniser.advanceTransition called with CharacterReferenceInData.

But fakeTokeniser.advanceTransition is a method we implement; we can have it record the state passed. So we can assert that fakeTokeniser.lastAdvancedState == TokeniserState.CharacterReferenceInData.

Similarly for other branches.

We'll need to test many branches.

Given time, we can write tests for each state covering at least one branch.

We'll also test static helper methods directly: handleDataEndTag, readData, readCharRef, readEndTag, handleDataDoubleEscapeTag.

For these, we can use FakeTokeniser and mock CharacterReader.

Now produce the test file.
